openingProblem.problem:
On 24 September 1931 the Japanese Cabinet declared that Japan “harbors no territorial designs in Manchuria”. Six months later the new state of Manchukuo was proclaimed there, and by 1941 Japanese troops stood in southern Indochina. Some observers blamed army officers who acted on their own; others pointed to Japan's economic crisis, or to a divided China that seemed easy to push around.

So what drove Japanese expansion: militarism and nationalism, economic need, or the weakness of China?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: which mattered most — militarism, economics or China's instability? Give one reason.
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which source or fact changed or confirmed your judgement?

chunks.title: How far did militarism and nationalism drive Japanese expansion?
chunks.body:
On the night of 18 September 1931 an explosion damaged the South Manchuria Railway near Mukden. The Japanese, who owned the railway, blamed Chinese nationalists and used the incident as the reason to invade Manchuria. The plan had been prepared by two officers of the Kwantung Army, Colonel Itagaki and Lieutenant Colonel Ishiwara; their commander, General Honjō, was at first appalled that it had gone ahead without his permission, but approved it after the act. Four days later the US Minister in China, Johnson, reported that the occupation was “an aggressive act by Japan apparently long planned”, not an accident or the work of “minor and irresponsible officials”.

This matters because it shows that expansion began with the army acting ahead of the government. The Cabinet still said that Japan had no territorial designs in Manchuria, yet Manchukuo was formally established on 1 March 1932.

The army's success then changed Japanese politics. In August 1932 the US Ambassador, Joseph Grew, reported that hostility to foreign nations was being built up deliberately “to strengthen the hand of the military in its Manchurian venture”, and that the military machine had been “built for war… and would welcome war”. Political violence followed: on 15 May 1932 young naval officers assassinated Prime Minister Inukai, and their light sentences strengthened militarism. In January 1933 the Japanese Ambassador told Secretary of State Stimson that no Cabinet which advocated a compromise over Manchukuo could survive in Japan. After the failed army coup of 26 February 1936, nineteen leaders were executed, but the military increased its control over the civilian government.

By 1937 nationalism was official policy. Prime Minister Konoe told the Diet that all policy must stem from “the spirit of the solemn and superb polity of our Empire” and called for perfecting national defence. Militarism therefore explains who started expansion and why civilian leaders found it hard to stop. It explains less about why so many Japanese supported it, which the economic crisis helps to answer.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Army officers, not the Cabinet, started the conquest of Manchuria.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Cabinet and later governments accepted and built on the army's action, so civilian leaders shared responsibility.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Political violence pushed governments towards the army's line after 1931.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Some violence (the 1936 coup) failed and was punished, so the army did not simply take over.

howItGetsAsked: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the role of militarism in Japanese expansion, 1931–1941.
To what extent did the Kwantung Army drive Japanese policy in Manchuria in 1931–1932?
Compare and contrast what two sources reveal about the role of the Japanese military.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Militarism started Japanese expansion and made it hard to reverse.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In September 1931 Kwantung Army officers staged the Mukden explosion, and the US Minister in China reported an aggressive act “apparently long planned”.
useItInAnEssay.explain: Because the army acted first, the government faced a fait accompli; after Inukai's assassination in May 1932 no Cabinet dared to compromise over Manchukuo.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Grew linked the military's power to the economic crisis, which suggests that militarism fed on wider discontent.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Militarism was the main cause of how expansion began, but not the only reason it gained support.

chunks.title: Did economic problems push Japan to expand?
chunks.body:
Japan's economy was in serious trouble in the early 1930s. In August 1932 Grew described farmers in a very bad plight, industries “at low ebb”, rising unemployment and a falling yen, with no money to be borrowed abroad. At the same time, he noted, millions of yen were being spent on the “Manchurian venture”, whose economic advantage was “highly problematical”. This matters because it shows two sides of the economic argument: hardship made people receptive to the promise of expansion, but expansion itself was costly.

Manchuria was resource-rich, and the Japanese state encouraged its people to settle there. Posters of the Manchuria Emigration Association (founded in 1935) called “Go to Manchuria!” and offered a government subsidy of 1,000 yen per household to young, fit farmers. In July 1937 Prime Minister Konoe told the Diet that Japan must develop its economic power on “the conception of Japan and Manchukuo as a single unit”. By late 1937 Japan had lost much of its gold reserves through a trade imbalance, and Konoe believed that exploiting northern China's resources was the only way to stop the deterioration. His statement of 22 December 1938 duly demanded that China give Japan facilities to develop its natural resources in North China and Inner Mongolia.

The need for raw materials grew as the war in China dragged on. In September 1940 Grew reported that some Japanese sought security by securing raw material sources and markets “entirely within Japanese control”. In August 1940 Japan's leaders announced a “Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere”, designed to free Japan from dependence on Western supplies. When Japan moved into southern Indochina in July 1941, Ambassador Nomura explained that Japan needed an “uninterrupted” supply of rice and raw materials.

Economics therefore explains why expansion attracted support and why it accelerated after 1937. But economic arguments were often used to justify decisions already taken by the army, and the war in China created many of the shortages that later expansion was meant to solve.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Economic crisis made expansion attractive in the early 1930s.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Grew also said the Manchurian venture was a costly drain, so expansion worsened the crisis rather than solving it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The search for raw materials drove the southward advance of 1940–1941.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Nomura's explanation was given to justify the move; the same memorandum also cites military security.

howItGetsAsked: Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent were economic problems the main cause of Japanese expansion?
Examine the importance of the need for raw materials in Japanese expansion, 1937–1941.
Compare and contrast what two sources reveal about Japan's economic motives.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Economic need made expansion popular and drove its later stages.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In 1932 Grew described farmers in a very bad plight and rising unemployment; in July 1941 Nomura said Japan needed an uninterrupted supply of rice and raw materials from Indochina.
useItInAnEssay.explain: Because Japan lacked raw materials and foreign credit, control of Manchuria, North China and later South-East Asia promised secure supplies.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Grew thought the economic advantage of Manchuria “highly problematical”, and the war in China itself created the shortages.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Economics explains the appeal and the direction of expansion more than its start.

chunks.title: Did China's divisions invite Japanese expansion?
chunks.body:
Background before 1931: China had been fragmented since the revolution of 1911. In 1926 the Kuomintang (Nationalist Party) launched the Northern Expedition under Chiang Kai-shek to reunify the country, and in December 1928 Zhang Xueliang, the ruler of Manchuria, accepted the Nationalist government's authority. But the Nationalists and the Communists had been fighting a civil war since 1927, and regional generals kept much of their power.

These divisions shaped Chinese and Japanese choices after 1931. Chiang believed that “the Japanese are a disease of the skin” while “the Communists are a disease of the heart”, and he ordered Zhang not to resist the invasion of Manchuria. Japan used China's condition to justify its actions. In October 1931 Tokyo blamed the crisis on “a deep-rooted anti-Japanese feeling in China”, organised, it said, by the Nationalist Party itself. At the League of Nations in February 1933 the Japanese delegate, Matsuoka, argued the opposite point too: that “the disorganized status of China” made the League's recommendations impossible to carry out. China was presented as both too hostile and too weak to be trusted with Manchuria.

The weakness was real but changing. In May 1937 the US Ambassador in China, Johnson, reported that Kwangsi province was still “virtually autonomous” and that the Communist problem could tear the country apart. Yet he also argued that Japanese pressure to separate five northern provinces had “done more than anything else to create in the Chinese people a desire for national unity”. In December 1936 two of Chiang's own generals seized him at Xi'an and demanded an end to the civil war and an alliance with the Communists against Japan; the crisis led to the Second United Front of 1937.

China's instability therefore made expansion look easy and gave Japan a ready justification. But it was not a cause on its own: Japan chose to exploit China's weakness, and by 1937 Japanese pressure was making China more united, not less, which helps explain why the war of 1937 did not end quickly.

argumentsThatWork.claim: China's civil war and regional divisions made it hard to resist Japan in 1931–1933.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Japanese pressure was itself creating Chinese unity by 1936–1937, so weakness was declining.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Japan used China's condition as a justification for expansion.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: These were arguments for an international audience; they do not prove that China's weakness caused Japanese decisions.

howItGetsAsked: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the importance of political instability in China as a cause of Japanese expansion.
To what extent was Chinese disunity responsible for the loss of Manchuria in 1931–1933?

useItInAnEssay.claim: China's divisions made expansion easier and gave Japan a justification.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Chiang ordered Zhang Xueliang not to resist in 1931 because he saw the Communists as the greater danger; Matsuoka cited “the disorganized status of China” at Geneva in 1933.
useItInAnEssay.explain: Because China was fighting a civil war, it could not defend Manchuria, and Japan could claim to be restoring order.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Johnson reported in 1937 that Japanese pressure was creating a desire for national unity in China.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Instability was a permissive condition that Japan exploited, not the driving cause.

chunks.title: What did the “new order” and the Axis link add to the causes of expansion?
chunks.body:
By 1938 Japan's leaders were explaining expansion as the building of a “new order in East Asia”. On 3 November 1938, after capturing Canton and the cities of Wuhan, the government announced that the Kuomintang government was now “a mere local régime” and that the ultimate purpose of the campaign was a new order resting on a “tripartite relationship” of Japan, Manchoukuo and China, with joint defence against Communism and close economic cohesion. On 22 December Konoe spelled out the price for China: recognise Manchoukuo, sign an anti-Comintern agreement, accept Japanese troops and open its natural resources to Japan. He insisted that Japan sought “neither territory nor indemnity”.

The United States rejected the idea. In a note dated 30 December 1938 it denied that any one power had a right “to prescribe what shall be the terms and conditions of a ‘new order’ in areas not under its sovereignty”. This matters because the new order was a cause of conflict as well as a description of Japan's aims: it closed the door to a compromise peace with Chiang and set Japan against the Western powers.

The ideological language connected Japan with Germany and Italy. Japan and Germany had signed the Anti-Comintern Pact on 25 November 1936, and Italy joined in 1937. German victories in 1940 then changed Japanese calculations. In September 1940 Grew reported that the military saw a “golden opportunity” to carry out its “dreams of expansion”, since the German victories had gone to their heads “like strong wine”. On 27 September 1940 the Tripartite Pact recognised Japan's leadership of a new order in Greater East Asia.

The new order and the Axis link therefore turned a war in China into a programme for the whole region. In January 1941 Secretary of State Hull told a committee of the House of Representatives that Japan aimed at a dominant position “in the entire region of the Western Pacific”. Ideas and alliances explain the scale of expansion after 1938; they do not explain its origins in 1931.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The “new order” turned the China war into a regional programme.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Konoe denied any territorial aims, so Japanese leaders presented it as cooperation, not conquest.

argumentsThatWork.claim: German victories in 1940 encouraged further expansion.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Grew also reported doubts in Japan about whether Germany would win.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The “new order” gave expansion a regional goal after 1938.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 3 November 1938 Japan declared that the ultimate purpose of its campaign was a new order of Japan, Manchoukuo and China.
useItInAnEssay.explain: Because this goal required China's submission and the exclusion of Western influence, it ruled out a compromise peace and set Japan against the United States.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the slogan followed the army's conquests and was partly a justification for them.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The new order explains the scale of expansion after 1938 more than its causes in 1931.

sourceSets.focus: Nationalism and militarism as causes of Japanese expansion

provenance.creator: Joseph C. Grew, US Ambassador to Japan
provenance.sourceType: private letter to the US Secretary of State, Henry Stimson
provenance.contextNote: “These facts” refers to Japan's economic difficulties, described earlier in the letter.

sources.text: Here in Japan the deliberate building up of public animosity against foreign nations in general and the United States in particular has doubtless a similar purpose—to strengthen the hand of the military in its Manchurian venture in the face of foreign, and especially American, opposition. … It seems to be primarily this military element … who believe that the best way to obscure these facts is to work the public into a patriotic and nationalistic fervor by representing foreign nations, particularly the United States, as trying to thwart Japan's efforts for alleged self-preservation. … The Japanese military machine … has been built for war, feels prepared for war and would welcome war. It has never yet been beaten and possesses unlimited self confidence.

provenance.creator: Unknown Japanese photographer
provenance.contextNote: Rebel soldiers led by Lieutenant Kurihara Yasuhide (centre, in a cape) during the attempted army coup in Tokyo that began on 26 February 1936.

provenance.creator: Prince Konoe (Konoye) Fumimaro, Prime Minister of Japan
provenance.sourceType: address to the Imperial Diet, as reported by the Domei news agency
provenance.contextNote: Fighting between Chinese and Japanese troops near Peiping (Beijing) had begun on 7 July 1937.

sources.text: “I desire to elucidate, first of all, the principle which underlies the endeavors of the Government to fulfill its immense responsibilities. This principle is to make all our policies stem from a single source, namely, the spirit of the solemn and superb polity of our Empire. … I am very grateful, however, that the Government has been accorded the united support of the nation at this critical moment. In sending troops to North China, of course, the Government has no other purpose … than to preserve the peace of East Asia. … In view of the current circumstances at home and abroad, it is of the most urgent necessity for us to perfect our national defense and develop the economic power of our country.”

provenance.creator: Johnson, US Minister in China
provenance.sourceType: telegram to the US Secretary of State, sent from Peiping (Beijing)
provenance.contextNote: Japanese forces had begun occupying South Manchuria after an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway near Mukden on 18 September 1931.

sources.text: 1. According to all information available to me here, I am driven to the conclusion that the forceful occupation of all strategic points in South Manchuria, including the taking over and operation of public utilities, banks, and in Mukden at least the functions of civil government, is an aggressive act by Japan apparently long planned and when decided upon most carefully and systematically put into effect. I find no evidence that these events were the result of accident nor were they the acts of minor and irresponsible officials. … 3. It is my conviction that the steps taken by Japan in Manchuria must fall within any definition of war and certainly may not be considered as a pacific means of settling a dispute with China …

questions.text: According to Source A, why was hostility towards foreign nations being built up in Japan?

points: To strengthen the hand of the military in its Manchurian venture.
To resist foreign, and especially American, opposition.
To hide (“obscure”) Japan's difficulties by working the public into patriotic and nationalistic fervour.
By presenting the United States as trying to thwart Japan's self-preservation.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about the position of the army in Japanese politics in 1936?

points: Junior officers were prepared to lead armed troops against the government in the capital.
The rebels appear organised and confident, marching openly with rifles.
Parts of the army saw themselves as entitled to act outside civilian control.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying the role of nationalism in Japanese expansion.

points: Value (origin): the Prime Minister's address to the Diet shows how the government officially presented its policy.
Value (content): it ties all policy to “the spirit of the solemn and superb polity of our Empire”, showing nationalism as official doctrine.
Limitation (purpose): a public speech meant to win support, so its claim that troops were sent only “to preserve the peace” may conceal real aims.
Limitation (origin): a news-agency report of a speech at the start of the war, so it shows intentions in July 1937 but not how policy developed.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources A and D reveal about the role of the Japanese military in Japanese expansion.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources present Japanese expansion as deliberate rather than accidental: Source A describes the “deliberate building up” of hostility, and Source D an act “apparently long planned”.

Both also point to the military as the driving force: A names “the military in its Manchurian venture”, and D sees a carefully executed military operation, not the work of “minor and irresponsible officials”.
However, Source A focuses on how the military manipulated public opinion at home, while Source D focuses on the operation in Manchuria and its legality, calling it war under the Kellogg Pact.
Source A also distinguishes a “military element” from the rest of Japan, whereas Source D treats the occupation simply as “an aggressive act by Japan”.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the view that militarism was the main cause of Japanese expansion between 1931 and 1941.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: Militarism was the main cause of how Japanese expansion began and why it was not reversed, although economic need and China's weakness explain why it attracted support.

Source D shows that the occupation of Manchuria was “apparently long planned”; in fact it was staged by Kwantung Army officers Itagaki and Ishiwara, and their own commander approved only after the act.

Source A explains how the military kept control: by stirring “patriotic and nationalistic fervor”. Political violence reinforced this; Prime Minister Inukai was assassinated by naval officers on 15 May 1932, and Source B shows armed rebels in Tokyo in February 1936.

Yet Source C shows a civilian Prime Minister, Konoe, presenting expansion as national policy with “the united support of the nation”, and Grew himself linked the military's power to Japan's economic crisis of farmers' hardship and unemployment.
Militarism was therefore the main cause in 1931–1936, but by 1937 expansion had become the policy of the whole state, supported by economic and nationalist arguments.

sourceSets.focus: Domestic economic problems and the drive for resources

provenance.creator: Joseph C. Grew, US Ambassador to Japan
provenance.sourceType: private letter to the US Secretary of State, Henry Stimson

sources.text: I believe that on the part of the Japanese it is a sign of weakness, not of strength. The internal economic and financial situation in Japan is serious and may become desperate. The plight of the farmers is very bad, many industries are at low ebb, unemployment is steadily increasing. The yen is falling and prices have not yet risen proportionately. Money cannot be obtained from abroad … Meanwhile millions of yen are being squandered to support the Manchurian venture, of which the eventual economic advantage is highly problematical, and when the full purport of these expenses becomes known to the people, in their own serious deprivation, there is no telling what effect it will create.

provenance.contextNote: The large slogan reads: “Open up Manchuria and Mongolia! Go to Manchuria!” The red panel reads: “Ministry of Colonial Affairs: recruitment of agricultural emigrants to Manchuria.” Smaller text offers a government subsidy of 1,000 yen per household to applicants aged 33 or under and physically strong.

provenance.creator: Welles, Acting US Secretary of State
provenance.sourceType: memorandum of a conversation with the Japanese Ambassador, Admiral Nomura
provenance.contextNote: Japan had just agreed with the French government at Vichy to send troops into southern Indochina.

sources.text: He stated that I was well aware of the critical economic situation of Japan and of the great difficulty which Japan had in procuring raw materials, particularly food supplies, from abroad. … He stated that Japan was now importing a million tons of rice a year from Indochina. He went on to say that one of the two reasons for the step taken was to assure to Japan an uninterrupted source of supply of rice and other food stuffs, which Indochina afforded, as well as an uninterrupted supply of other raw materials which they required from that region. … The Ambassador then said that the second reason for the occupation undertaken was the need for military security. He stated that Japan believed that certain foreign powers were bent upon a policy of encirclement of Japan …

provenance.creator: Joseph C. Grew, US Ambassador to Japan
provenance.sourceType: telegram to the US Secretary of State (State Department paraphrase)
provenance.contextNote: German forces had defeated France in June 1940.

sources.text: 3. Whatever the intentions of the present Japanese Government may be there cannot be any doubt that the military and other elements in Japan see in the present world situation a “golden opportunity” to carry their dreams of expansion into effect; the German victories, like strong wine, have gone to their heads … 4. … They see that Britain and the United States are steadily drawing closer together in mutual defense measures … They tend on the one hand to emphasize the potential danger facing Japan from the United States and Great Britain eventually acting together in positive action … They furnish cogent arguments on the other hand for those Japanese elements who seek political and economic security by securing raw material sources and markets entirely within Japanese control.

questions.text: According to Source A, what economic problems did Japan face in 1932?

points: The plight of the farmers was very bad.
Many industries were at low ebb.
Unemployment was steadily increasing.
The yen was falling and money could not be obtained from abroad.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about Japanese aims in Manchuria?

points: Manchuria was seen as land to be settled and farmed by Japanese emigrants.
The Japanese state actively sponsored settlement, with a government ministry and a subsidy of 1,000 yen per household.
It sought young, fit settlers, suggesting long-term colonisation.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source D for a historian studying the economic motives for Japanese expansion.

points: Value (origin): a telegram from the US Ambassador in Tokyo to his own government, who was well placed to report the mood of Japanese political circles.
Value (content): it identifies a group seeking security through raw materials and markets “entirely within Japanese control”, linking economics to expansion.
Limitation (purpose): written to advise Washington on a firmer policy, so it may stress Japanese opportunism.
Limitation (origin): a State Department paraphrase of an outsider's judgement; it cannot show how Japanese leaders weighed economic against strategic motives.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources C and D reveal about Japan's need for raw materials.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources link Japanese expansion to raw materials: Source C reports Nomura's wish for “an uninterrupted supply of other raw materials”, and Source D describes elements seeking raw material sources “entirely within Japanese control”.
Both also connect economic needs to security: C mentions fear of “encirclement”, and D the danger of Britain and the United States acting together.

However, Source C presents the need as defensive and urgent (food and a million tons of rice a year), while Source D presents expansion as opportunism, a “golden opportunity” produced by German victories.
Source C gives a Japanese explanation, reported by an American official, whereas Source D is entirely the American Ambassador's own interpretation.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent were economic problems the main cause of Japanese expansion between 1931 and 1941?

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: Economic problems were an important cause because they made expansion attractive and shaped its direction, but they were not the main cause of its start in 1931.

Source A shows a serious crisis in 1932, with farmers in a very bad plight and rising unemployment, and Source B shows the state offering 1,000 yen per household to settle Manchuria, so expansion promised land and work.
After 1937 the need grew: by late 1937 Japan had lost much of its gold reserves, and Sources C and D show the search for raw materials behind the move into southern Indochina in July 1941.
However, Source A also says the economic advantage of Manchuria was “highly problematical”, and the invasion itself was started by Kwantung Army officers in September 1931, not by economic planners.
Economic problems therefore explain the appeal and the later direction of expansion more than its origins, which lay with the army.

provenance.sourceType: despatch to the US Secretary of State, sent from Nanking
provenance.contextNote: In December 1936 Chiang Kai-shek had been detained at Xi'an (Sian) by two of his own generals.

sources.text: For the past several years there has been growing among Chinese, irrespective of their political and personal inclinations, a feeling that the continuance of Chiang Kai-shek in power is essential to the salvation of the Chinese nation. This feeling has been intensified and its growth promoted by aggressive Japanese activities in and with reference to China … Japanese pressure exerted to partition China by alienating five northern provinces has done more than anything else to create in the Chinese people a desire for national unity … While Chiang Kai-shek has enjoyed success in nominally unifying China … the transitional period from so called feudalism and individualism has not completely passed. … Kwangsi is virtually an autonomous province.

provenance.creator: Gilbert, US Consul at Geneva
provenance.sourceType: telegram to the US Secretary of State reporting the League of Nations Assembly
provenance.contextNote: Matsuoka Yōsuke led the Japanese delegation. The draft report was based on the findings of the League's Lytton Commission.

sources.text: 4. Matsuoka declared that Japan could not accept the draft report. Then in a forceful speech he appealed to the Assembly not to accept the draft report basing his contention on: (1) The special historical and present situation in Manchuria was not sufficiently understood by the members of the Assembly for them to pronounce a competent opinion; (2) The disorganized status of China rendered the recommendations inapplicable and their carrying out impossible, in particular that no mere technical assistance to China would suffice to restore order …

questions.text: According to Source A, who was responsible for the Manchurian crisis?

points: The Chinese Government.
A deep-rooted anti-Japanese feeling in China.
The Nationalist Party, which directed the anti-Japanese movement as national policy.
Chinese provocation, which compelled Japanese troops to act in self-defence.

questions.text: What is the message of Source B?

points: Chinese people should reject both Chiang Kai-shek and communism (Stalin).
Ending the war and “saving the nation” means accepting a new, pro-Japanese leadership.
Chiang is portrayed as violent and defeated.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying the political situation in China before the war of 1937.

points: Value (origin): the US Ambassador in Nanking had direct access to Chinese officials and reported regularly on Chinese politics.
Value (content): it shows both continuing division (Kwangsi “virtually autonomous”) and growing national unity under pressure from Japan.
Limitation (purpose): written to assess what would happen if Chiang died, so it may overstate his importance.
Limitation (origin): an outside observer's view, written two months before the war began, so it cannot show how Chinese groups acted once war came.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources A and D reveal about how Japan presented the situation in China.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources show Japan blaming conditions in China for the crisis rather than its own actions: Source A blames “a deep-rooted anti-Japanese feeling”, and Source D Matsuoka's claim that China's “disorganized status” made the League's plan impossible.
Both reject outside judgement of Japan's actions: A says responsibility “naturally lies with the Chinese Government”, and D records Matsuoka's refusal to accept the League's report.

However, they describe China in opposite ways. Source A presents an organised campaign directed by the Nationalist Party “as an instrument of national policy”, while Source D presents a China too disorganised to keep order.
Source A is a direct Japanese government statement, whereas Source D is a US consul's summary of a Japanese speech.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the importance of political instability in China as a cause of Japanese expansion between 1931 and 1941.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: China's instability was an important permissive cause: it made expansion easier and gave Japan a justification, but Japan chose to exploit it.

Source C shows that even in 1937 China was not fully unified, with Kwangsi “virtually autonomous”. In 1931 Chiang, fighting a civil war against the Communists since 1927, ordered Zhang Xueliang not to resist in Manchuria.
Japan used this condition: Sources A and D blame Chinese agitation and disorder, and Source B shows propaganda in occupied China calling for Chiang's overthrow and an end to communism.

However, Source C also argues that Japanese pressure had created a desire for national unity; after the Xi'an incident of December 1936 the Nationalists and Communists moved towards cooperation, yet Japan still expanded in 1937.
Instability was therefore a condition and a justification rather than the driving cause, which lay in Japanese decisions.

sourceSets.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
sourceSets.focus: The “new order in East Asia” and alignment with Germany and Italy

provenance.creator: Japanese Government
provenance.sourceType: statement released by the Foreign Office for publication

sources.text: By the august virtue of His Majesty, our naval and military forces have captured Canton and the three cities of Wuhan; and all the vital areas of China have thus fallen into our hands. The Kuomintang Government exists no longer except as a mere local régime. … What Japan seeks is the establishment of a new order which will insure the permanent stability of East Asia. In this lies the ultimate purpose of our present military campaign. This new order has for its foundation a tripartite relationship of mutual aid and co-ordination between Japan, Manchoukuo and China in political, economic, cultural and other fields. Its object is to secure international justice, to perfect the joint defence against Communism, and to create a new culture and realize a close economic cohesion throughout East Asia.

provenance.creator: Unknown Japanese artist
provenance.contextNote: The title reads “Good friends: three countries”. The portraits are labelled Hitler, Prime Minister Konoe and Mussolini. Children wave Japanese, German and Italian flags.

provenance.creator: US Government
provenance.sourceType: note delivered by Ambassador Grew to the Japanese Foreign Minister, Arita

sources.text: The admonition that enjoyment by the nationals of the United States of non-discriminatory treatment in China—a general and well established right—is henceforth to be contingent upon an admission by the Government of the United States of the validity of the conception of Japanese authorities of a “new situation” and a “new order” in East Asia, is, in the opinion of this Government, highly paradoxical. … This Government is well aware that the situation has changed. This Government is also well aware that many of the changes have been brought about by the action of Japan. This Government does not admit, however, that there is need or warrant for any one Power to take upon itself to prescribe what shall be the terms and conditions of a “new order” in areas not under its sovereignty …

provenance.creator: Prince Konoe (Konoye) Fumimaro, Prime Minister of Japan
provenance.sourceType: statement released by the Japanese Foreign Office

sources.text: Japan, China and Manchoukuo will be united by the common aim of establishing the new order in East Asia and of realizing a relationship of neighbourly amity, common defence against Communism, and economic co-operation. For that purpose it is necessary first of all that China should cast aside all narrow and prejudiced views belonging to the past and do away with the folly of anti-Japanism, and resentment regarding Manchoukuo. … Japan demands … that China … should extend to Japan facilities for the development of China's natural resources, especially in the regions of North China and Inner Mongolia. … what she seeks is neither territory nor indemnity for the costs of military operations.

questions.text: According to Source A, what were the aims of Japan's “new order”?

points: The permanent stability of East Asia.
A tripartite relationship of Japan, Manchoukuo and China.
Joint defence against Communism.
A new culture and close economic cohesion throughout East Asia.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about Japan's relations with Germany and Italy?

points: They are presented as a friendship between equal partners, with the three leaders side by side.
The image aims to make the alignment popular with ordinary Japanese, using children and flags.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source D for a historian studying Japanese aims in China.

points: Value (origin): an official statement by the Prime Minister sets out the government's declared terms for China.
Value (content): it lists concrete demands (recognising Manchoukuo, access to resources in North China and Inner Mongolia).
Limitation (purpose): released for audiences at home and abroad, so the claim that Japan sought “neither territory nor indemnity” is meant to reassure.
Limitation (content): it shows declared aims in December 1938, not the private views of the army, which controlled policy in occupied China.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources A and D reveal about Japan's “new order in East Asia”.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both sources describe the new order as a union of Japan, Manchoukuo and China, with “joint defence against Communism” in A and “common defence against Communism” in D.
Both stress economic links: A speaks of “close economic cohesion”, and D of “economic co-operation” and access to China's natural resources.
However, Source A emphasises military conquest, with “all the vital areas of China” in Japanese hands, while Source D emphasises cooperation and denies seeking territory.
Source D also sets specific conditions for China, such as recognising Manchoukuo and giving up “anti-Japanism”, whereas A gives only general objects.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent was the aim of a “new order” in East Asia a cause of Japanese expansion between 1937 and 1941?

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, uses the sources and accurate own knowledge as evidence, and reaches a judgement.

segments.text: The aim of a new order was an important cause of the scale of expansion after 1938, although it grew out of conquests that had other causes.
Sources A and D show that by late 1938 Japan's declared aim was a new order of Japan, Manchoukuo and China, which required China's submission and access to its resources.

Source C shows why this aim widened the conflict: the United States denied any power the right to prescribe a new order outside its sovereignty. Source B reflects the link with Germany and Italy, formalised in the Tripartite Pact of 27 September 1940, which recognised Japan's leadership in Greater East Asia.

However, the new order was proclaimed only after the capture of Wuhan and Canton, so it partly justified conquests already made; economic need, such as the search for raw materials in Indochina in 1941, also drove the advance south.
The new order was therefore a major cause of the widening of expansion after 1938, but a justification as much as a motive.
